label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Jess texted me last night to say, more or less, “It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.”

I know. And before I say anything else: I know she said it because she loves me, not because she thinks history doesn’t matter. We met student teaching in 2012. She has known me long enough to recognize when I’m about to turn a manageable problem into a principle I can’t climb down from. That is useful information to have about a friend. Annoying, but useful.

Half the group chat agreed with her. I started typing a reply, deleted it, started another, and realized I was about to make everybody read fifteen texts when one excessively long blog post would do.

So, Jess, this is mostly for you. You don’t have to agree with me. I just want to explain why I don’t think I can quietly drop this.

For the last four years, I’ve given my juniors in US History II an oral history assignment about Boston’s busing and desegregation years, 1974–76. Two sections. A ten-minute recorded interview with someone in their family or neighborhood, followed by a two-page reflection.

That sounds fairly ordinary written out like that. In practice, it depends very much on whose kitchen you’re sitting in.

This is the history of the city these kids live in. It happened on streets they know, in neighborhoods where their families still live. Their textbook gives it about a paragraph. An interview can’t give them the whole history either, but it can get them asking questions that the paragraph doesn’t.

Until now, there hadn’t been a complaint.

The parent who emailed my principal, copying a school committee member, said the assignment “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” My principal wants me to let it go. We’re meeting with the parent on Thursday, November 19, at 3:15.

I don’t want to turn that meeting into a showdown. I also don’t intend to walk in and agree to abandon the project.

But the parent has a point about pressure. I need to say that plainly, because otherwise everything that follows sounds like a defense I prepared without listening.

I’m the teacher. I assign the work and give the grade. A kid can hear “interview someone in your family” as an instruction to ask questions they don’t feel able to ask, even if I think I’ve made room for choice. They may have to live with the consequences of that conversation long after I’ve read their reflection and moved on to the next unit.

I don’t get to decide that a difficult conversation at home is worth it on their behalf.

So I’m going to propose keeping the project and adding a clear alternate route: interview a librarian or archivist, or work with recordings from previous years where we have permission to use them. Nobody should have to interview a relative to complete this assignment. Nobody should have to explain their family situation to me to get another option.

That’s a change I should have thought through sooner. I can admit that without concluding that the whole thing was a mistake.

Part of why I want to keep it is a moment from 2023 that I still think about.

A student I’ll call D. interviewed his grandmother. She had driven a school bus in South Boston in 1974. She’d never told anyone in the family about it.

He played about forty seconds of the recording for the class.

Afterward, nobody said anything for what felt like a full minute. I can’t tell you exactly what every student was thinking, and I don’t want to turn their silence into evidence for whatever I happen to believe. But I remember how unusual it was. A room full of juniors, listening to somebody’s grandmother, then sitting with what they’d heard.

She had been there. D. hadn’t known. Now he did, and so did the people sitting next to him.

That matters to me.

Last year, another student learned that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year.

I hesitate even to put those two facts next to each other. Her being upset wasn’t a teaching achievement. A good paper doesn’t settle the question of what it cost her to write it, and I don’t know everything that happened after she went home.

But I also don’t think the fact that she was upset means she would have been better off never knowing.

That’s the difficult part. There isn’t a rule that makes it easy.

I’ve caught myself thinking that the kids who are uncomfortable with this history are the ones who most need to encounter it. Sometimes I think that’s true. Sometimes I think it’s a very convenient thing for a teacher to believe. It can let me treat any objection as proof that I’m doing important work.

I need to be more careful than that. Discomfort can mean a student is reconsidering something. It can also mean I’ve put them in a situation they shouldn’t have been required to enter. I have to pay attention to the difference, and I won’t always get it right.

What I can do is make sure there’s a way to do the historical work without requiring access to someone’s family wounds.

The “judge their grandparents” part of the complaint bothers me, though. Understanding what happened does involve judgment. We can ask students to consider context and conflicting memories without asking them to pretend that throwing rocks at children on a bus was morally ambiguous.

That doesn’t mean an assignment should end with a verdict on someone’s entire family. Loving a person and learning something awful about what they did is hard. Adults struggle with it. I’m not expecting a sixteen-year-old to resolve it neatly in two pages.

I do want them to have somewhere to ask about it.

And yes, Jess, I could get burned.

I’ve had tenure since 2021. That gives me protection, and I’m not going to write this as if I’m risking instant unemployment by disagreeing with my principal. But he still controls my schedule. He still has a say in who gets AP. There are plenty of ways for work to become less pleasant without anybody firing you.

I’m scared of that. A little more than I’ve probably let on in the chat.

I like my job. I want a decent working relationship with my principal. I don’t want to become the teacher whose name makes everybody tired when it appears in an email. I would much rather have a normal Thursday.

But if I drop this now, it won’t be because I’ve decided the assignment can’t be improved. I already have changes I want to make. It’ll be because one complaint made keeping it feel dangerous.

I don’t think I’d feel good about that decision once the immediate relief wore off.

You’re right that it’s one assignment. I know there are other ways to teach this history. I’m not claiming this project is irreplaceable, or that every teacher who decided differently would be wrong. I’m saying I’ve watched students do work through it that I want future students to have the chance to do, with better choices and clearer limits than I’ve given them before.

That seems worth a meeting. Even one I’m dreading.

I’m not angry with you for wanting me to protect myself. Please keep being the friend who tells me when I’m making my life harder. You’ve been doing it since 2012; I’d hate to waste all that experience.

I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting. You can ask how it went before telling me you warned me. I know you’ll want to.
